claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by a dynamically generated coherent oxide layer formed during sliding.
The dynamically generated oxide forms primarily through selective oxidation of an oxide-forming element such as Al.
The oxide acts as a load-bearing, low-shear interface that mitigates direct metal-metal contact and reduces wear.
The proposed initial coating is equiatomic or near-equiatomic CoCrFeNiAl.
The proposed as-deposited coating has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The proposed as-deposited coating has no preformed oxide layer.
Increasing Al content should enhance the ability of the coating to form a continuous, robust oxide layer during wear.
Pre-oxidation should enhance the coating's protective oxide-forming attributes during wear.
Tribo-oxidation is active in ambient air at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
The protective wear-surface film is predominantly alumina-rich, coherent, and mechanically robust.
The oxide film redistributes applied loads and reduces shear at the contact interface.
Frictional heat during sliding accelerates localized oxidation.
Sufficient Al enables rapid formation of a continuous, adherent tribo-oxide layer.
The continuous tribo-oxide lowers wear by reducing direct metal contact and friction.
Lower-Al coatings form a less continuous oxide film and consequently exhibit higher wear.
Coatings designed to promote coherent oxide formation should exhibit approximately a 30–50% reduction in wear rate relative to the baseline.
Coatings designed to promote coherent oxide formation should exhibit a more stable and lower friction coefficient.
A lower-Al or non-pre-oxidized baseline produces a thinner or more discontinuous oxide film under identical wear conditions.
Suppressing oxidation through an inert atmosphere or very low temperature diminishes the proposed oxide-mediated mechanism.
The quantitative wear benefit is composition-dependent.
